title: Taking over as director of the Rum Boogie show band
summary: With Marl Young writing and failing to get the music played, Cobb takes the baton on opening night, becomes the show's director and earns $60 a week.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Like Marl Young was writing some of that show, wasn't he?

Marl Young was the man that was writing for the show when we were first with him, and we were his men, and he used to pull his hair out because we weren't playing the music. And Charlie Glenn would say, "We're gonna open the show tonight." I'll give you the tape we got from Chicago; it was my wife's birthday, that's how I can't forget it. She's an Augustite, too ... one week apart. August third. Hear me

talking to you? August third. And we opened up -- at Joe's Joe Ziggy Johnson got the chorus girls, Marl doing the writing, (unintelligible), we got a guy in St. Louis writing, and I'll tell you what good readers we were -- we could spell a little bit, but this was a big time show; we ain't never hit nothing this big time before in our life! And nobody could play. I ain't never directed a band in my life. My right hand to God.

But Charlie Glenn sat on the railing on the side; he said, "Now time is passing," and he said, "Somebody has to open the show tonight. And Maur is pulling his hair out. And I'm listening, and I'm watching everything he was saying, so when it got so critical, I came out, I said, "Well, just give me an opportunity to do something. Let me help", because I'm carrying my wife with me; I got my automobile out, away from home, got rent to pay back here -- still holding the house, and here I am, they gonna put us out before we get in.
I got up there and I directed that band and was wobbly kneed, but desperate.
I thought Maur directed it sometimes.

Maur directed it the first night, and then after that, he turned it loose, and I had to take over. But he wanted to turn it loose that day, and I got up and I did what I saw him do. But he said, "I'll take it tonight, to

open. All he was doing was writing for the show; not directing the band. But when he directed that band, man, I told him that I'd take day I took it over, I watched everything he did, and from the second night on, I had it. You know what I ended up doing? Every time the show changed, we were off on Monday nights, the damn house band, and every time they had a new show, they had a new house band, I would come in on Mondays and rehearse the house band for what we had done already.
Charlie Glenn gave me $10 and a bottle of liquor. I'm telling you the God's truth. Ten dollars and a bottle of liquor. Now I'm making $60 a week.
And you were well pleased with that.

I was happy! Let me tell you how happy I was. I first went in with my wife's aunt and it was rent free. Then we moved where we could be by ourselves, to a girlfriend of mine from Houston, and she had a 4-room place down between 63rd and 64th Street, and she was never there, and we had access to her cooking, and she paid $24 a month -- and we paid half of it. Twelve dollars. Don't you know I had $60 a week -- I had it free.
And when I left to go join Lionel Hampton's band, I had some money in my pocket; I had saved some money.
